questions.q: What is lateral movement, as this lesson defines it?
options: Using access gained at an initial foothold to reach further, higher-value systems
Patching vulnerabilities across multiple systems at once
Moving data between regions for compliance reasons
Rotating credentials on a fixed schedule
questions.explain: Lateral movement is what turns a single compromised foothold into a wider breach — using what was gained at that foothold to reach further systems.

questions.q: Why does pass-the-hash work against machines that share the same local administrator account and password?
options: Because the plaintext password is stored in a public registry
Because a cached credential hash dumped from one compromised machine is valid against every other machine using the same account and password
Because hashes automatically expire after one use, making them safe to reuse once
Because antivirus software caches hashes for convenience
questions.explain: Pass-the-hash reuses a cached credential hash directly; if the same local admin account and password exist on many machines, one dumped hash authenticates to all of them.

questions.q: Why does token or ticket theft sidestep MFA, according to this lesson?
options: MFA only applies to administrator accounts, never regular users
Tokens are encrypted so MFA cannot be applied to them at all
MFA already happened once at login, and the stolen token is proof that it happened — it is not a fresh check at the moment the token is replayed
MFA is disabled automatically once a session token is issued
questions.explain: A token represents a session that already proved identity once; replaying a stolen token elsewhere doesn't trigger a new MFA prompt because the proof-of-authentication already happened.

questions.q: What is the specific purpose of a Privileged Access Workstation (PAW)?
options: A workstation given to every employee regardless of role
A virtual machine used only for running antivirus scans
A shared kiosk machine used by multiple administrators for convenience
A dedicated, locked-down machine used only for privileged administrative tasks, kept separate from everyday devices used for email and browsing
questions.explain: A PAW is the one place privileged credentials are ever used, deliberately separated from general-purpose devices to prevent privileged credentials from being exposed on a commonly compromised machine.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that no single control fully stops lateral movement on its own?
options: Because lateral movement cannot be stopped by any technical control, only by policy
Because each control — unique local admin passwords, PAWs and credential tiering, micro-segmentation — closes a specific technique but leaves other techniques open, so they must be layered together
Because MFA alone is sufficient to stop every technique described in this lesson
Because firewalls automatically block all forms of lateral movement by default
questions.explain: Unique local admin passwords close pass-the-hash but not token theft; PAWs and tiering close the privileged-credential path but not movement between ordinary workstations — each control is matched to a specific technique and must be layered with the others.
